source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck & Boshuizen (2013) The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: learning to reason about legal cases
finding: Core claim of the subfield tested directly. Worked examples beat problem solving for law-case reasoning, a less structured task, for novices and also for advanced students. No expertise reversal.
numbers: 75 first-year and 36 third-year law students; 2x2x2 design (worked examples vs problem solving x process steps x expertise); n=18-19 per cell for first-year, n=9 per cell for third-year. Test score 0-100 on a new ownership-transfer case.
quote: worked examples were more effective for learning than problem-solving, both for novice and advanced students
limits: Task is 'less structured', not truly open: cases were set at first-year level, two learning cases and one test case on one legal theme, short session. Reversal not tested as a formal interaction; years analysed separately.
agent_relevance: A scaffold should not assume that open or ill-structured tasks need no worked examples. For a hard task whose steps can be shown, show a solved case first.

source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck & Boshuizen (2013) The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: learning to reason about legal cases
finding: First-year result: huge worked example effect on test performance, with less time and less effort during learning.
numbers: Test score M=58.63 (SD 27.74) worked examples vs M=8.59 (SD 4.06) problem solving; F(1,68)=105.22, p<.001, Cohen f=1.24. Learning time 568.47 s vs 1146.15 s (F(1,70)=58.13, f=0.75). Mental effort (9-point scale) 5.46 vs 6.39 (F(1,67)=15.44, f=0.42). Effort on the test task did not differ.
limits: Problem-solving novices scored near floor (about 9 of 100), so floor shapes the effect size. Variances unequal; Welch test gave the same result (F=120.8). Outliers removed from effort and time data.
agent_relevance: Without any guidance a novice in an unfamiliar rule-heavy task fails almost completely. This is the baseline that an open-mode agent must beat with some support.

source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck & Boshuizen (2013) The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: learning to reason about legal cases
finding: Third-year (advanced) result: worked examples still clearly better. Advanced students had far more prior knowledge but did not reverse.
numbers: Prior knowledge test (max 34): third-year M=17.12 vs first-year M=8.86, d=2.75. Third-year test score M=82.28 (SD 18.11) worked examples vs M=37.06 (SD 26.71) problem solving; F(1,32)=37.03, p<.001, f=1.02. Learning time 427.36 s vs 975.58 s (f=1.00). Effort not different (F(1,32)=2.22, p=.15).
limits: Third-year n=9 per cell; post hoc power .64 (authors). Mann-Whitney confirmed (Z=4.13, r=.688). Third-years in problem solving (M 37) were still far below their worked-example peers.
agent_relevance: Competence in a domain does not remove the value of seeing a full solved case when the solution has many variable parts.

source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck & Boshuizen (2013) The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: learning to reason about legal cases
finding: Process steps alone (a Toulmin-style checklist: grounds, warrants, backings, rebuttals, qualifier, conclusion) did not help learning and cost time.
numbers: First-year problem solving: learning time 1460.72 s with steps vs 831.58 s without (t(34)=4.68, p<.001, d=1.56), but test score 8.33 vs 8.88 (no gain). Steps raised effort only in problem-solving cells (main effect f=.24). For third-years no effect of steps (F<1).
limits: Steps were given as a list and diagram; novices had to find out what each step means. Only one process model (Toulmin) was tried.
agent_relevance: A generic 'think in these steps' prompt is not the same as a worked example. A schema that lists steps without showing them worked out may add cost with no gain on novel tasks.

source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck & Boshuizen (2013) The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: learning to reason about legal cases
finding: Authors' explanation for no reversal: less structured tasks have many variable elements that cannot be automated, so expertise takes longer to build and examples stay useful longer.
numbers: Prior knowledge differed by d=2.75 yet the benefit of examples persisted. Third-year students did better on the test case overall (M=59.67 vs 34.76, Z=3.71, r=.35) and invested less effort in learning (4.46 vs 5.75).
quote: less structured tasks take longer to master, and hence, examples may remain effective for a longer period of time
limits: Explanation is speculative: they could not tell whether examples helped law content, search in the civil code, or reasoning itself. No transfer case. They suggest fading should drop easy parts earlier than variable parts.
agent_relevance: Fading from solved to open should be per sub-skill, not per task: fade the recurrent parts first and keep modelling the variable parts.

source: Rourke & Sweller (2009) The worked-example effect using ill-defined problems: learning to recognise designers' styles
finding: Earlier study cited by Nievelstein: worked examples helped art and design students learn to recognise designers' styles. Second-year students gained relatively more than first-year students, so no expertise reversal was seen.
numbers: Not read in full (publisher page blocked, 403). Details come only from Nievelstein et al. (2013). OpenAlex lists 146 citations.
limits: Second-hand summary only. Authors attributed the pattern to second years having more visual literacy. Numbers not verified by us.
agent_relevance: Shows the worked example effect was already claimed for an ill-defined recognition task before the legal study.

source: Kyun, Kalyuga & Sweller (2013) The effect of worked examples when learning to write essays in English literature
finding: Three experiments with Korean university students writing English-literature essays (ill-structured domain). Model answers helped, and the benefit grew as student knowledge fell. This pattern matches expertise reversal.
numbers: Abstract only (via OpenAlex): 3 experiments; Exp 1 most knowledgeable, Exp 3 least; effect increased with decreasing knowledge. Sample sizes and effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract-level. Students were learners of English as a foreign language, so language knowledge is confounded with domain knowledge.
agent_relevance: A counter-point to Nievelstein: in creative writing, examples helped novices most and probably less for experts. Expect expertise to matter in open tasks.

source: Schworm & Renkl (2007) Learning argumentation skills through the use of prompts for self-explaining examples
finding: Examples of argumentation taught declarative knowledge. To teach the skill, prompts had to direct attention to the argumentation principles, not to the topic of the example.
numbers: Abstract only (via OpenAlex): N=71 student teachers, 4 conditions that differ in whether and how self-explanation prompts supported example processing. Effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract-level. Student teachers, one skill (two-sided argumentation).
agent_relevance: In open tasks the example has two content levels (topic and skill). The agent must be pointed at the pattern, not the content.

source: Renkl (2023) Using worked examples for ill-structured learning content (in Overson et al., In Their Own Words, APA Div. 2)
finding: Renkl defines ill-structured content as problems with no algorithm, only heuristics that help but do not guarantee success. He sorts tested cases into four groups: ill-structured parts of well-structured domains (proof, experimenting), ill-structured domains (law, medicine, essays, negotiation, designer styles), cross-domain skills (argumentation, concept mapping, cooperation, learning journals), teacher education.
numbers: No new data. Lists studies: Hilbert et al. 2008; Reiss et al. 2008; Nievelstein et al. 2013; Stark et al. 2011; Kyun et al. 2013; Gentner et al. 2003; Rourke & Sweller 2009; Hefter et al. 2014/2018/2019; Martin et al. 2020/2022.
quote: most learning content from school mathematics is well-structured. However, finding proofs is ill-structured learning content
limits: Practitioner chapter by a main researcher in the area; selective, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Gives a usable taxonomy: the unit of analysis is the learning content (a heuristic skill), not the whole domain. Maps onto our open mode: the agent skill is the heuristic, e.g. 'argue both sides'.

source: Renkl (2023) Using worked examples for ill-structured learning content (in Overson et al., In Their Own Words, APA Div. 2)
finding: Same explanation as for well-structured tasks: novices who try to solve at once are overloaded, use superficial strategies (copy an old solution and change numbers), and learn little. So study principles first, then examples, then problems.
numbers: Cited baseline: worked example effect first shown by Sweller & Cooper 1985, Cooper & Sweller 1987, Tarmizi & Sweller 1988 on algebra and similar.
limits: Explanation (extraneous load from weak methods) is argued for ill-structured content by analogy; the chapter reports no direct load measure for it.
agent_relevance: Order for open mode: short principles, then solved cases with the principle named, then open attempts.

source: Renkl (2023) Using worked examples for ill-structured learning content (in Overson et al., In Their Own Words, APA Div. 2)
finding: Two content levels: a learning domain (the skill, e.g. argument structure) and an exemplifying domain (the topic, e.g. lynx or global warming). Weak prior knowledge in the exemplifying domain gave poor learning of the skill. Prompts that pointed at the topic hurt skill learning.
numbers: Hilbert et al. 2004, 2008: low exemplifying-domain knowledge gave poor outcomes. Schworm & Renkl 2007: topic-directed prompts hampered learning. Hilbert et al. 2008: fill-in gaps in geometry (exemplifying domain) harmed learning to prove.
quote: prompts directing the learners' attention primarily to the exemplifying domain hamper knowledge acquisition in the learning domain
limits: Numbers for these studies are not given in the chapter.
agent_relevance: When showing the agent a worked case for an open task, keep the topic easy and mark the reasoning moves. A hard topic or a topic-focused prompt pulls attention away from the move being modelled.

source: Renkl (2023) Using worked examples for ill-structured learning content (in Overson et al., In Their Own Words, APA Div. 2)
finding: Practical boundary conditions for ill-structured examples: use pre-structured self-explanation prompts first and open ones later; text can beat video; avoid completion gaps that attract attention to the topic; skills need many sessions.
numbers: Hefter et al. 2019: no learning advantage for video over text or graphic novel, but less time for text and graphic novel. Martin et al. 2022: 90-min seminar, 3-4 min video segments plus pre-structured prompts worked best, but no transfer to new unsegmented videos.
limits: One-session interventions; the author calls them kick-off interventions, not full skill acquisition.
agent_relevance: Support given inside the scaffold may not transfer when removed. Expect gains to depend on the support staying present, so fade it gradually and test without it.

source: Renkl (2023) Using worked examples for ill-structured learning content (in Overson et al., In Their Own Words, APA Div. 2)
finding: Heuristic worked examples for proof finding: four phases (conjecture, statement, exploration, deductive chain) shown with fictitious students thinking aloud. The examples are long, 10+ pages, and include self-explanation prompts.
numbers: Reiss et al. 2008 classroom study with 8th graders and Hilbert et al. 2008 are the sources. Exemplifying domain: geometry (parallelogram proof). Numbers not given in the chapter.
limits: Secondhand. Examples are costly to write.
agent_relevance: A model of a worked example for an open task: show the thinking aloud, label each phase, and ask which phase it is. This is close to a state-labelled reasoning trace.

source: Van Gog & Rummel (2010) Example-based learning: integrating cognitive and social-cognitive research perspectives
finding: Review noting that worked examples have been mostly used for highly structured tasks, while modelling examples (video of a person) cover less structured skills like writing, assertive communication, collaboration, self-regulation. Lists less structured worked-example studies as of 2010.
numbers: Listed: instructional design model (Hoogveld 2005), argumentation (Schworm & Renkl 2007), concept maps (Hilbert & Renkl 2009), designer styles (Rourke & Sweller 2009), legal cases (Nievelstein, then in press). Notes heterogeneity: in some studies weaker students learned more from weak models; in Grosse & Renkl 2007 only students with more prior knowledge gained from erroneous examples.
quote: difficult to draw definitive conclusions about what works, when, and for whom
limits: Review, not data; text read only around the relevant passages (pages 158-159, 168).
agent_relevance: Two example types exist for open tasks: worked-out ideal solutions and models of natural, imperfect performance. Our agent may need both.

source: Schmidt, Loyens, van Gog & Paas (2007) Problem-based learning is compatible with human cognitive architecture
finding: Source of the objection Nievelstein tests: high-guidance formats shown to work on well-structured tasks might not carry over to less structured tasks.
numbers: Not opened. Known here only through Nievelstein et al. 2013, p. 119.
limits: Second-hand. This is a commentary, not data.
agent_relevance: Names the sceptical hypothesis (guidance fails on ill-structured tasks) that the later studies mostly did not support.

source: van Peppen, Verkoeijen, Heijltjes, Janssen, Koopmans & van Gog (2018) Effects of self-explaining on learning and transfer of critical thinking skills
finding: Boundary case: for semi-structured reasoning tasks (syllogism, base-rate, Wason selection, conjunction), adding self-explanation prompts to instruction plus practice did not help, and hurt on the Wason/conjunction practiced tasks.
numbers: N=79 first-year applied-university students; pretest, immediate and 2-week delayed posttest. Instruction and practice raised performance in both groups and the gain was kept. Prompts had no effect on transfer. Abstract reports a negative prompt effect on practiced Wason and conjunction tasks; one printed statistic is F(1,37)=7.66, p=.009, partial eta2=.172 (condition mapping not checked against tables).
limits: I read the abstract and parts of the results; the mapping of that statistic to a condition was not verified. Short-term study.
agent_relevance: Not every generative or self-explaining add-on helps. Extra reflection steps in the scaffold can lower accuracy on tasks where instruction already works.

source: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez, Jiang, Wadhwa, Singhal, Zhao, Ye, Mahowald & Durrett (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning (ICLR 2025)
finding: LLM analogue of the task-type limit. Meta-analysis of over 100 CoT papers plus own tests on 20 datasets and 14 models: CoT helps strongly on math, symbolic and logic tasks, and little elsewhere.
numbers: Literature mean CoT gain: symbolic +14.2, math +12.3, logical +6.9 points. Top three categories 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. All other categories 56.8 vs 56.1. On MMLU, as much as 95% of the CoT gain comes from questions with an equals sign.
quote: CoT gives strong performance benefits primarily on tasks involving math or logic, with much smaller gains on other types of tasks
limits: Compute not matched between CoT and direct answer (authors say a fair test would match compute). Benchmarks are mostly fixed-answer, so open-ended generation is under-sampled.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a step-by-step operator should be routed by task type. For open mode it gives about zero expected gain from plain CoT.

source: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez, Jiang, Wadhwa, Singhal, Zhao, Ye, Mahowald & Durrett (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning (ICLR 2025)
finding: Own experiments by reasoning category show the same split: large CoT gain on math, small on knowledge and commonsense, mid on symbolic. Most non-math gains are not significant after correction.
numbers: Per-category averages across 14 models (appendix table, direct vs CoT, %): commonsense 74.8 vs 75.7; knowledge 73.3 vs 77.5; math 22.6 vs 50.2; symbolic 45.2 vs 56.1; soft reasoning 58.3 vs 60.3. Bonferroni p<0.00027: about 32% (59) of the apparent gains in knowledge/soft/commonsense were significant, 26 of them on MMLU and MMLU-Pro.
limits: Column order of the appendix table assumed from its header. Main figure is zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Soft reasoning (the nearest benchmark class to ill-structured work) gets about +2 points from CoT. Do not spend tokens on long chains there.

source: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez, Jiang, Wadhwa, Singhal, Zhao, Ye, Mahowald & Durrett (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning (ICLR 2025)
finding: CoT gains come mostly from carrying out symbolic steps, not from planning. A symbolic solver beats CoT on those tasks. Authors suggest using CoT selectively.
numbers: Planning and execution were separated: Plan + tool solver beat Plan + CoT solver and CoT on average across models on math and logic sets (figure values not extracted).
limits: Only the main text claim was read; per-model figures not transcribed.
agent_relevance: In a scaffold, structured steps with a tool or checker help well-defined tasks. For open tasks the tool route does not exist, so other support is needed.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo & Griffiths (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse (ICML 2025)
finding: Tested CoT on six tasks where deliberation hurts humans. In three, CoT clearly hurt models: implicit statistical learning, visual recognition where words fit poorly, and learning labels with exceptions. In the other three, effects were mixed or positive.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning (artificial grammar): up to 36.3% absolute accuracy drop for OpenAI o1-preview versus GPT-4o; a table row shows GPT-4o 87.50% zero-shot vs 64.40% CoT (-23.10, p<0.0001); consistent drops in eight other LLMs. Face recognition: all six vision-language models dropped. Exceptions task: CoT raised the number of rounds to learn labels by up to 331%.
quote: CoT reduces performance in three archetypes: implicit statistical learning, language ill-suited to represent stimuli, learning labels with exceptions
limits: Task-by-task heuristic, not a classifier. Where models hold priors humans lack (logic) or long context (preference aggregation), CoT did not hurt.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist for when to switch thinking off: pattern-feel tasks, perceptual tasks, rule-with-exceptions tasks. Fits a guardrail that routes by task type.

source: Min, Lyu, Holtzman, Artetxe, Lewis, Hajishirzi & Zettlemoyer (2022) Rethinking the role of demonstrations: what makes in-context learning work?
finding: For classification and multiple-choice tasks, demonstrations help mainly by showing the label space, the input distribution and the format. Correct labels barely matter.
numbers: Replacing gold labels with random labels lowered performance only marginally over 12 models including GPT-3, in classification and multi-choice sets. Gold-label demonstrations clearly beat no demonstrations.
quote: replacing labels in demonstrations with random labels barely hurts performance
limits: Closed-label tasks only. The result may not hold for generation or reasoning where the content of the solution is the point.
agent_relevance: In LLMs an example may act as a format and distribution cue, unlike a human worked example, which teaches steps. For open tasks, examples may anchor form more than ideas.

source: Xiao, Zhao & Huang (2025) The role of diversity in in-context learning for large language models
finding: Choosing in-context examples for diversity (not just similarity to the query) helps most on harder tasks (math, code) and under distribution shift.
numbers: Llama-3.1, Gemma-2, Mistral-v0.3 families. On GeoQuery diversity-aware top-K selection gave at least a 7% absolute accuracy gain; benefits bigger on harder examples.
limits: Tasks have fixed correct answers; the work is not about creative output.
agent_relevance: Example choice matters more as tasks get harder. If our agent retrieves worked cases, pick varied ones, not only the nearest.

source: Anderson, Shah & Kreminski (2024) Homogenization effects of large language models on human creative ideation (C&C 2024)
finding: In an open ideation task, using ChatGPT as a creativity aid made the group's ideas more alike than using a card deck (Oblique Strategies), even though each person's own range was no narrower.
numbers: 36 participants. Group-level similarity to the mean embedding: ChatGPT M=.24 vs card deck M=.28, t(32)=2.154, p=.038, d=.47. About one more idea per person (about 15% more). Users felt less responsible for ideas, d=.67, p=.003.
limits: Human users, not model prompting. Small N, one ideation tool comparison. Authors did not rate idea quality.
agent_relevance: Shows the open-task risk of model help: more output, same ideas. An agent that gets model suggestions as examples may converge on one pattern.

source: Padmakumar & He (2024) Does writing with language models reduce content diversity? (ICLR 2024)
finding: In a controlled essay task, co-writing with a feedback-tuned model (InstructGPT) lowered diversity, but co-writing with the base model (GPT-3) did not.
numbers: 3 groups (solo, GPT-3, InstructGPT), 10 essays per topic per group, 10 topics, 300 essays total. Essays with InstructGPT showed higher homogenization and lower lexical and key-point diversity; user-written text stayed unchanged; the effect came from the model's contributed text.
limits: Argumentative essays only, one model pair, crowdworkers from Upwork.
agent_relevance: Tuning for helpfulness may cost diversity, so model-made 'examples' or suggestions for open tasks should be sampled with care.

source: Ibrahim, Azad & Baten (2026) Anchorless diversification for parallel LLM ideation
finding: For open-ended idea generation, what raises diversity is structure in the request, not example ideas: one planning call that lists broad semantic directions, then parallel generation spread across them, gives top-tier diversity per token.
numbers: Three creative task families. Population-referential instruction ('stand out from other responses') raised semantic diversity while keeping quality proxies; direction stratification reached top-tier final-pool diversity with high gain per 100k pipeline tokens; anchored regeneration advantage shrinks under full-pipeline token counting.
limits: May 2026 preprint; quality is only proxied by automatic measures. Number of models: three (details not extracted).
agent_relevance: A candidate support for open mode that is not a worked example: plan the space first, then generate across it.

source: Hilbert, Renkl, Kessler & Reiss (2008) Learning to prove in geometry: learning from heuristic examples and how it can be supported
finding: Heuristic examples for proving worked, and gap-filling in geometry content plus self-explanation prompts hurt skill learning (as reported by Renkl 2023).
numbers: Not opened. Facts taken from Renkl (2023): low exemplifying-domain knowledge gave poor outcomes; gaps in geometry expressions were detrimental. URL given is the secondary source.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Warns that active-completion extras can backfire when they point at the wrong content level.

source: Cross-source synthesis (Nievelstein 2013; Sprague 2025; Min 2022; Ibrahim 2026), made by this research agent
finding: Reading across the sources: in humans, solved cases help on less structured tasks when principles are named and the topic is easy. In LLMs, plain step-by-step thinking gives little on soft tasks, demonstrations mostly set format, and open generation gains from structural moves like direction planning.
numbers: Evidence points: human worked-example effect f=1.24 (novice) and f=1.02 (advanced) on law cases; CoT on soft reasoning about +2 points (58.3 to 60.3); random-label demonstrations lose little.
limits: Synthesis, not a finding of one study. No LLM study found that tests worked examples versus problem solving on an ill-structured task with measured learning gains.
agent_relevance: Gap: nobody has measured worked-example support for an LLM on an ill-structured task. We would have to run it ourselves.
